passages.t: A tall young man and his father's donkeys
passages.happening:
A powerful man of the tribe of Benjamin named Kish has a son named Saul, ‘choice and handsome’, and ‘a head taller than any of the people’ (verse 2).

Kish's donkeys wander off, and he sends Saul with a servant to look for them (verse 3). They search through the hill country of Ephraim, the land of Shalishah, the region of Shaalim and the land of Benjamin, and find nothing (verse 4). When they reach the land of Zuph, Saul wants to turn back, “or my father will stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us” (verse 5).

The servant has an idea. “Look,” said the servant, “in this city there is a man of God who is highly respected; everything he says surely comes to pass” (verse 6). Perhaps he will tell them which way to go. Saul worries that they have no gift for him, and the servant has the answer to that too: he has a quarter shekel of silver (verses 7-8).

The narrator adds a note for later readers: ‘For the prophet of today was formerly called the seer’ (verse 9). “Good,” said Saul to his servant. “Come, let us go” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 8 ended with the LORD telling Samuel to give the people a king. Chapter 9 begins with a farm errand. The contrast is deliberate. Israel asked for a king to fight its battles, and God answers through a young man who cannot find his father's donkeys and has to be told where to go by his servant.

Benjamin was a small tribe, set on a strip of land between Ephraim to the north and Judah to the south. It had nearly been wiped out in the civil war at the end of Judges, which may be why Saul will call it the smallest tribe. A king from Benjamin also had advantages, since it lay between the strong northern and southern tribes. Saul's hometown, Gibeah, is traditionally placed at Tell el-Ful, just north of Jerusalem, though other sites have been proposed.

Not all the places Saul passes through can be found today. Zuph links with Samuel's family, since one of Samuel's ancestors was named Zuph (1:1). The town where Saul meets Samuel is never named, and whether it was Samuel's home at Ramah is debated.

Saul is impressive to look at, and passive. The servant has the idea, the money and the knowledge of the man of God. It was normal in that world to ask a seer about practical things like lost animals, and to bring a gift. The quarter shekel of silver comes from a time before coins, when payment was made by weighing out metal.

The note about the seer explains an older word for readers who knew only the newer one. It is one of several signs that the book was written some time after the events.
passages.later:
The memory of Benjamin's near destruction lies behind Saul's humility. At the end of Judges the tribes had grieved, “Today a tribe is cut off from Israel” (Judges 21:6).

The old word seer lasted. Centuries later a priest of Bethel told the prophet Amos, “Go away, you seer!” (Amos 7:12).
passages.asks: Saul went out to look for donkeys and was being led toward a crown. Ask where ordinary errands in your life may be part of something larger than you can see. And ask whose small suggestion, like the servant's, you may need to listen to.

passages.happening:
Climbing the hill to the town, Saul and his servant meet some young women going out to draw water and ask whether the seer is there. He is, they say, and they should hurry: there is a sacrifice today on the high place, and the people will not eat until he comes (verses 11-13).

As they enter the town, Samuel is coming toward them (verse 14). The day before, the LORD had told him, “At this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you are to anoint him leader over My people Israel; he will save them from the hand of the Philistines. For I have looked upon My people, because their cry has come to Me” (verse 16). When Samuel sees Saul, the LORD tells him, “Here is the man of whom I spoke; he shall rule over My people” (verse 17).

Saul asks Samuel where the seer's house is. “I am the seer,” Samuel replied (verse 19). He invites Saul to eat with him, tells him the donkeys have been found, and asks a strange question: “And upon whom is all the desire of Israel, if not upon you and all your father’s house?” (verse 20).

Saul replied, “Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin? So why would you say such a thing to me?” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The reader knows more than Saul does. The narrator tells what the LORD said to Samuel the day before, so the reader watches Saul walk into God's plan without knowing it. Many scholars compare the story to an old pattern in folk tales, in which a young man goes looking for lost animals and finds a kingdom.

The key word is find. Saul cannot find the donkeys, the young women say he will find the seer, and the donkeys are found. The search for lost animals becomes the way God finds Saul.

God's words to Samuel echo the exodus. He has seen his people and heard their cry, and he sends someone to save them. The people demanded a king, but the choice of the king remains God's, as the law had said it must.

God tells Samuel to anoint Saul as leader, in Hebrew nagid, not as king. Many scholars think the word means something like the one God has appointed, a ruler answerable to God.

The high place was a local open-air place of worship, often on high ground. Before the temple was built in Jerusalem, sacrifice at such places was common and not condemned. Only later did the prophets and the books of Kings treat them as rivals to the temple and places of idolatry.

Saul's humble answer sounds like Gideon's when he was called. Samuel's question about the desire of Israel hints at the kingship, and Saul does not yet understand.
passages.later:
God's words to Samuel echo what he said to Moses at the burning bush: “I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their oppressors” (Exodus 3:7).

Gideon had answered his own call in the same way: “how can I save Israel? Indeed, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father’s house” (Judges 6:15).
passages.hard:
If God knew that Saul would fail, why did he choose him?

The question is natural, since the LORD will later reject Saul and say that he regrets making him king (15:11, 35). Several answers have been given. Some stress that Saul was truly suited to the task in many ways: he was humble at first, he received the Spirit, and he won real victories. His failure came from his own choices, not from a fault in God's choice. Others see Saul as the kind of king the people asked for, impressive to look at and a warrior, and read his reign as a lesson in the limits of choosing by appearance, set against David, chosen because God looks at the heart (16:7). Still others note that God's plan took in both Saul's reign and its failure, preparing the way for David without excusing Saul's disobedience.

These views can be held together. The Bible often presents God as ruling over outcomes while holding people fully responsible for their choices, and it does not claim to explain how the two fit.
passages.asks: Saul said he was from the smallest tribe and the least clan. Ask whether you have ever thought yourself too small for what God asked of you. And ask whether humility at the start of something is enough to keep you faithful when it grows.

passages.t: A place at the head of the table
passages.happening:
Samuel brings Saul and his servant into the hall and seats them at the head of the guests, about thirty in all (verse 22). He tells the cook to bring the portion he had set aside, and the cook sets before Saul ‘the leg and what was attached to it’ (verse 24). It has been kept for him, Samuel says, for this very occasion.

After the meal they come down from the high place, and Samuel speaks with Saul on the roof of his house (verse 25). Just before dawn Samuel calls to him on the roof, “Get ready, and I will send you on your way!” (verse 26).

As they go down to the edge of the town, Samuel tells Saul to send the servant on ahead, ‘but you stay for a while, and I will reveal to you the word of God’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
A sacrificial meal was a shared feast. The meat of a peace offering was eaten by the worshipers, and where people sat and what they were given showed their standing. Samuel puts Saul at the head of about thirty guests and gives him a portion kept in reserve, the leg. The right thigh was usually the priest's portion, so the guests would have noticed that this stranger had been singled out.

Sleeping on a flat roof was common in the warm season, and a roof was also a private place to talk.

The chapter ends at the edge of the town, before dawn, with the servant gone ahead. Saul still does not know why he has been honored. The word of God is about to be spoken to him, in private.
passages.later: The law gave the right thigh of the peace offering to the priest: “And you are to give the right thigh to the priest as a contribution from your peace offering” (Leviticus 7:32).
passages.asks: Samuel set Saul at the head of the table before Saul knew why. Ask how you carry honor that comes before you have done anything to earn it. And ask whether you are ready to stay behind when someone says, ‘I will reveal to you the word of God.’
